questions.q: Why is knowing that 'port 21 is open' alone nearly useless to a pentester?
options: Dozens of FTP server implementations and versions exist, and whether it's a real finding depends on exactly which one is running
Port 21 is never actually associated with FTP services
Open ports are always false positives generated by the scanner
Nmap cannot detect open ports without authentication
questions.explain: An open port number by itself says nothing about risk. Enumeration exists to turn that port into an exact answer — which software, which version — because that's what can actually be cross-referenced against known vulnerabilities.

questions.q: What does Nmap's -sV flag actually do?
options: It brute-forces login credentials against every open port
It automatically exploits any vulnerable version it finds
It only works against web servers running HTTP
It sends probes from the nmap-service-probes database and matches responses against known signatures to identify software and version
questions.explain: -sV works by sending a sequence of probes and comparing the responses against Nmap's signature database, which is how it distinguishes Apache from nginx and extracts a specific version string.

questions.q: Why would a pentester manually grab a banner with `nc -nv target 21` after -sV already reported a version?
options: To read the service's raw, unprompted greeting directly, confirming the automated result rather than trusting it blindly
Banner grabbing is required before Nmap is allowed to run at all
nc automatically patches the vulnerable service it connects to
Because -sV cannot detect FTP services under any circumstances
questions.explain: A raw connection with netcat or telnet reads exactly what the service sends with no interpretation layer in between, which is a useful manual check when a finding matters and you want to verify what an automated tool reported.

questions.q: What does running `nmap -sV -sC -p- target` add beyond plain version detection?
options: It skips version detection entirely in favor of OS fingerprinting
It performs a denial-of-service test against the target
It disables all port scanning and only runs vulnerability scripts
It runs Nmap's default NSE script set, pulling extra detail like HTTP titles, SSL certificate info, or SMB OS info
questions.explain: -sC runs Nmap's default, generally safe NSE scripts, which extract additional detail version detection alone doesn't surface, such as HTTP response headers or SMB OS discovery info.

questions.q: Why would a pentester run enum4linux -a against a Windows host instead of relying on Nmap alone?
options: enum4linux replaces the need for any TCP port scan
It can pull SMB-specific detail like share names, domain info, and user lists that a general port scanner isn't built to extract
It is a required step before Nmap is permitted to run
It only works on Linux targets, never Windows
questions.explain: Protocol-specific enumeration tools like enum4linux go deeper into one specific service (SMB) than a general-purpose scanner does, pulling shares, domain/workgroup info, and sometimes user lists or password policy.
